entry: Endocrine gland at the base of the brain, about the size of a kidney bean. It sits in the sella turcica, a bony depression in the sphenoid bone, and is controlled by the hypothalamus. Its anterior lobe (adenohypophysis) produces and secretes several [[Hormone|hormones]], while its posterior lobe (neurohypophysis) secretes hormones made in the hypothalamus. Pituitary hormones help control growth, [[Blood pressure|blood pressure]], energy management, the [[Sex organ|sex organs]], the [[Thyroid|thyroid gland]], [[Metabolism|metabolism]], water and salt balance at the kidneys, pain relief, and aspects of [[Pregnancy|pregnancy]], [[Childbirth|childbirth]] and [[Breastfeeding|breastfeeding]].

American computer animation studio in Emeryville, California, a subsidiary of Walt Disney Studios. Founded in 1979 as the Graphics Group of Lucasfilm's computer division, it became a corporation in 1986, with funding from [[Steve Jobs]], who became its majority shareholder. Disney completed its acquisition in May 2006. Pixar has produced 31 feature films, starting with *Toy Story* (1995), the first fully computer-animated feature film. As of July 2023, its films had grossed over $17 billion worldwide. Eleven of its films have won the [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]] for Best Animated Feature since 2001.

Smallest addressable element of a raster image. In a display device, dot matrix printer or ASCII art, a pixel is the smallest element whose output can generally be controlled independently. Pixels are usually arranged in a regular two-dimensional grid, each storing one or more numerical values that represent a sample of an image. In color imaging, a pixel is commonly represented by red, green and blue (RGB) components, or by cyan, magenta, yellow and black (CMYK). The German word *Bildpunkt* ("picture point") appeared in an 1888 patent, and the word was first published in 1965 by Frederic C. Billingsley of JPL, describing scanned images from space probes. [[Software]] on early consumer computers was rendered at low resolution, producing graphics called pixel art, especially in video games. Modern displays render far more pixels, necessitating large measurements such as the megapixel (one million pixels).

American [[Alternative rock|alternative rock]] band formed in Boston, Massachusetts, in 1986. Known for dynamic loud-quiet-loud shifts and the surreal lyrics of its principal songwriter, Black Francis, the band released the mini-LP *Come On Pilgrim* (1987) and the albums *Surfer Rosa* (1988), *Doolittle* (1989), *Bossanova* (1990) and *Trompe le Monde* (1991). It disbanded in 1993 after modest success in the U.S. and greater success in the United Kingdom and Europe. Its sound influenced [[Nirvana (band)|Nirvana]], [[Radiohead]] and [[Weezer]]. The band reunited in 2004, and the albums *Head Carrier* (2016), *Beneath the Eyrie* (2019) and *Doggerel* (2022) followed.

Italian dish of a flat base of leavened [[Wheat|wheat]]-based dough topped with [[Tomato|tomato]], [[Cheese|cheese]] and other ingredients. It is baked at a high temperature, traditionally in a wood-fired oven. The term *pizza* was first recorded in AD 997 in a [[Latin|Latin]] manuscript from Gaeta, in [[Lazio|Lazio]]. Raffaele Esposito is often credited with creating the modern version in [[Naples|Naples]] at the end of the 19th century. In 2009 Neapolitan pizza was registered with the European Union as a traditional speciality guaranteed dish, and in 2017 the art of making it was included on [[UNESCO]]'s list of intangible cultural heritage. Pizza is sold in restaurants, pizzerias, by delivery and as street food, and frozen or as kits in grocery stores. In 2017 the world pizza market was US$128 billion; in the U.S., it was $44 billion spread over 76,000 pizzerias. Between 2017 and March 2020, about 11% of the U.S. population ate pizza on a given day.

Spanish opera singer, conductor and arts administrator. Primarily a lirico-spinto tenor for most of his career, he was acclaimed for roles such as Cavaradossi and Otello before moving into baritone parts in the early 2010s. He recorded more than a hundred complete operas and won fourteen [[Grammy Awards|Grammy]] and Latin Grammy Awards. In 1990 he began singing with [[Luciano Pavarotti]] and José Carreras as The Three Tenors. He was general director of the Los Angeles Opera from 2003 to 2019 and founded the Operalia singing competition. In 2019, over 20 women made allegations of [[Sexual harassment|sexual harassment]] and misconduct against him, dating back to the 1980s. Investigations by the American Guild of Musical Artists and the Los Angeles Opera concluded that he had engaged in inappropriate conduct; Domingo denied abusing his position or coercing anyone. He resigned from U.S. administrative roles and continued to perform mainly in Europe and Latin America.

A [[Medicine|medicine]] or treatment intended to appear genuine to its recipient but having no pharmaceutical effect. Common placebos include inert tablets, such as sugar pills, inert injections such as saline, and sham surgery. In randomized clinical trials, the change in a control group given a placebo is the placebo response, and the difference between this and the result of no treatment is the placebo effect. Placebos are used to test treatments while keeping participants and clinicians from knowing who receives the treatment under test. The idea of a placebo effect was discussed in 18th-century psychology but became more prominent in the 20th century. A 2001 [[Meta-analysis|meta-analysis]] of trials in 40 medical conditions found a significant effect only for [[Pain|pain]], and a 2010 Cochrane review likewise found effects apparent only in subjective, continuous measures. Disguising placebos as active treatment raises ethical concerns, because it bypasses [[Consent|informed consent]]. The term derives from the [[Latin|Latin]] *placebo*, meaning "shall be pleasing."

Temporary embryonic and fetal organ connecting the [[Fetus|fetus]] to the [[Uterus|uterine]] wall. It develops from the blastocyst shortly after implantation and enables exchange of nutrients, gases and waste between the separate maternal and fetal circulations. It is also an endocrine organ, producing [[Hormone|hormones]] that regulate maternal and fetal physiology during [[Pregnancy|pregnancy]]. In humans it is expelled from the uterus after birth, together with a thin layer of maternal decidual tissue. Placentas are a defining feature of [[Mammal|placental mammals]] and are also found in [[Marsupial|marsupials]] and some non-mammals. Mammalian placentas probably first evolved about 150 million to 166 million years ago. The protein syncytin has an RNA signature in its genome that has led to the hypothesis that it originated from an ancient [[Virus|retrovirus]]. In humans the placenta averages 22 cm in length and typically weighs approximately 500 grams.

Extinct group of armored, jawed prehistoric [[Vertebrate|vertebrate]] fishes, known from Silurian and Devonian fossils. Their head and thorax were covered by articulated armored plates, from which the name derives (Greek *plax*, "plate", and *derma*, "skin"), while the rest of the body was scaled or naked. Placoderms were among the first jawed fish and the first vertebrates to have true [[Tooth|teeth]]. They were also the first fish group to develop pelvic fins, the homologous precursor of hindlimbs in [[Tetrapod|tetrapods]]. Fossils of three genera about 380 million years old represent the oldest known examples of live birth. They included some of the first vertebrate [[Apex predator|apex predators]], such as the large *Dunkleosteus terrelli*, 3.5–4.1 meters (11–13 ft) long. All placoderms became extinct at the end-Devonian Hangenberg event 358.9 million years ago, leaving niches for the osteichthyan and chondrichthyan survivors that radiated during the [[Carboniferous|Carboniferous]].

Representation of another person's language, thoughts, ideas or expressions as one's own original work. In many countries and cultures it is considered a violation of academic integrity and journalistic [[Ethics|ethics]], punishable by sanctions such as suspension, expulsion, fines or imprisonment. It is typically not in itself a crime, but it may be punished in court where it overlaps with copyright infringement, violation of moral rights or [[Tort|torts]]. The [[Latin|Latin]] word *plagiarius* ("kidnapper") was used in the 1st century by the Roman poet Martial for copying another's creative work. The English word *plagiary* was introduced in 1601 by dramatist [[Ben Jonson]], and *plagiarism* around 1620. Historians Polybius and [[Pliny the Elder]] condemned plagiarism, as did [[Vitruvius]].

Infectious disease caused by the bacterium *Yersinia pestis*. Symptoms, which usually begin one to seven days after exposure, include fever, weakness, headache and black lips. Bubonic plague affects the lymph nodes, making them swell; pneumonic plague infects the lungs; and septicemic plague infects the blood. The bubonic and septicemic forms are generally spread by [[Flea|flea]] bites or by handling an infected animal, whereas pneumonic plague spreads between people through infectious droplets. If infected, treatment is with [[Antibiotic|antibiotics]] and supportive care. Globally, about 600 cases are reported a year, with the most in 2017 in the [[Democratic Republic of the Congo]], [[Madagascar]] and [[Peru]]. The best known historical outbreak is the [[Black Death]] of the 14th century, which caused massive loss of life in Europe.

Common name for a group of four [[Flatfish|flatfish]] species: European, American, Alaskan and scale-eye plaice. The European plaice (*Pleuronectes platessa*) is the most important commercial plaice and the principal commercial flatfish in Europe. It lives on sandy bottoms from the [[Barents Sea]] to the Mediterranean, feeds on [[Polychaete|polychaetes]], [[Crustacean|crustaceans]] and bivalves, and has a maximum recorded length of 100 cm (39 in). The American plaice ranges from southern Labrador to Rhode Island and is generally smaller, with a maximum recorded length of 82.6 cm (32.5 in); the Northwest Atlantic Fisheries Organization considers it overfished, with no signs of recovery. Alaska plaice can live for up to 30 years, while the scale-eye plaice is found in the northern Pacific, from the [[Sea of Okhotsk|Sea of Okhotsk]] to Japan and Korea. The name derives from late Latin *platessa*, meaning flatfish, which comes from the Greek *platys* ("broad").

Flat expanse of land with few rapid or steep changes in elevation. Plains occur as lowlands along valleys or at the base of mountains, as coastal plains, and as plateaus or uplands. They are one of the major landforms on Earth, present on all continents and covering more than one-third of the world's land area. Natural vegetation can include [[Prairie|prairies]], grassland, forests, savanna, [[Tundra|tundra]] and desert biomes. Where soils were deposited as sediments on plains, they may be deep and fertile, and their flatness facilitates mechanized [[Agriculture|agriculture]]. Plains can also form from flowing [[Lava|lava]] or from erosion of hills or mountains. Types include [[Abyssal plain|abyssal plains]], flat or very gently sloping areas of the deep ocean basin, and glacial plains formed by the movement of [[Glacier|glaciers]]. The Latin *planitia* is used in naming plains on other planets, such as Hellas Planitia on [[Mars]].

Fundamental physical constant of foundational importance in [[Quantum mechanics|quantum mechanics]], denoted *h*. A [[Photon|photon]]'s energy is equal to its frequency multiplied by the constant. [[Max Planck]] postulated it in 1900 as a proportionality constant needed to explain experimental [[Black-body radiation|black-body radiation]], and later called it the "quantum of action". In [[Metrology|metrology]] it is used with other constants to define the [[Kilogram|kilogram]]; in SI units it has the exact value *h* = 6.62607015×10⁻³⁴ J⋅Hz⁻¹. The reduced Planck constant, ℏ (h-bar), equals *h* divided by 2π and is commonly used in quantum physics equations.

Formula describing the spectral density of electromagnetic radiation emitted by a [[Black-body radiation|black body]] in thermal equilibrium at a given temperature. At the end of the 19th century, physicists could not explain the observed black-body spectrum, which diverged at higher frequencies from theoretical predictions. In 1900 [[Max Planck]] derived the formula by assuming that an oscillator could change its energy only in minimal increments proportional to frequency. Planck originally saw this as a mathematical artifice, but [[Albert Einstein]] built on his work. Higher temperatures raise the total radiated energy and shift the spectral peak to shorter wavelengths.

System of [[Natural units|natural units]] defined exclusively in terms of four universal physical constants: c, G, ħ and kB. Expressing one of these constants in Planck units gives a numerical value of 1. The units are defined using properties of free space rather than a prototype object. They were originally proposed in 1899 by German physicist [[Max Planck]] and are relevant to research on unified theories such as [[Quantum gravity|quantum gravity]]. The Planck scale refers to quantities of space, time and energy similar in magnitude to the Planck units, with particle energies of around 10¹⁹ GeV, time intervals of around 10⁻⁴³ s and lengths of around 10⁻³⁵ m. At this scale, the predictions of the [[Standard Model]], quantum field theory and general relativity are not expected to apply. One example is the conditions in the first 10⁻⁴³ seconds of the universe after the [[Big Bang]], approximately 13.8 billion years ago.

Two-dimensional space or flat surface that extends indefinitely. A plane is the two-dimensional analogue of a [[Point (geometry)|point]] (zero dimensions), a [[Line (geometry)|line]] (one dimension) and three-dimensional space. Several notions exist. The Euclidean plane follows [[Euclidean geometry|Euclidean geometry]] and the parallel postulate. A projective plane adds "points at infinity" so that every pair of lines meets in exactly one point, and an elliptic plane adds a metric to it. A hyperbolic plane obeys hyperbolic geometry and has negative curvature. Forgetting all structure except [[Topology|topology]] gives the topological plane, homeomorphic to an open disk. Adding a compatible field structure gives the complex plane, the setting of [[Complex analysis|complex analysis]]. Planes are fundamental in mathematics, geometry, trigonometry, [[Graph theory|graph theory]] and graphing.

Hand tool for shaping [[Wood|wood]] by forcing a cutting iron, or blade, over its surface. Planes can flatten, reduce the thickness of, or smooth a rough or non-flat piece of [[Lumber|lumber]] or timber. The blade is set at an angle in a firm body, and the sole guides the cutter so that it removes only the highest parts of the surface; a longer sole gives a more consistently flat result. Japanese planes are pulled toward the body rather than pushed away. The earliest known woodworking planes were found in [[Pompeii]], and other Roman examples have been found in Britain and Germany. One Roman plane found in [[Cologne]] has a body made entirely of [[Bronze|bronze]]. In the mid-1860s, Leonard Bailey began producing cast-iron-bodied planes; his design is still manufactured by Stanley Black & Decker.

Hypothetical ninth planet in the outer [[Solar System]]. Its gravity could explain the clustering of orbits of extreme [[Trans-Neptunian object|trans-Neptunian objects]] (ETNOs), which average more than 250 astronomical units (AU) from the Sun. Some astronomers attribute the clustering to observational biases instead. Astronomers Konstantin Batygin and Michael Brown have suggested that the planet may be the core of a giant planet ejected by [[Jupiter]]. Its estimated orbit was updated to 290±30 AU in 2025. Sky surveys have not detected it, and it remains purely conjectural unless observed.

Type of [[Nebula|emission nebula]] consisting of an expanding, glowing shell of ionized gas ejected from [[Red giant|red giant]] stars late in their lives. The name describes the planet-like round shape seen through early telescopes, though these objects are unrelated to planets. Planetary nebulae form at the end of the life of a star of about 1–8 solar masses, and the Sun is expected to form one. They last perhaps a few tens of millennia. Once the red giant's atmosphere has dissipated, ultraviolet radiation from the exposed hot core, the planetary nebula nucleus, ionizes the ejected material, causing it to glow. They probably play a crucial role in the chemical evolution of the [[Milky Way|Milky Way]] by expelling elements into the [[Interstellar medium|interstellar medium]]. About one-fifth are roughly spherical, but the majority are not, and the mechanisms producing their varied shapes are not well understood. The [[Ring Nebula|Ring Nebula]] is a well-known example.

Set of non-stellar bodies gravitationally bound to, and in orbit around, a star or star system. Such a system generally includes planets, and may include [[Dwarf planet|dwarf planets]], asteroids, natural satellites, comets, meteoroids and circumstellar discs. By convention, systems are named after their host star, as with the [[Solar System|Solar System]], named after Sol, Latin for Sun. The International Astronomical Union defines a planetary system as planets orbiting one or more stars, brown dwarfs or stellar remnants. As of 8 October 2026, there were 6,534 confirmed [[Exoplanet|exoplanets]] in 4,908 planetary systems, 1,080 of which had more than one planet. [[Nicolaus Copernicus|Nicolaus Copernicus]]'s *De revolutionibus orbium coelestium* (1543) presented the first mathematically predictive heliocentric model of a planetary system. The first confirmed exoplanet, found in 1992, orbited the [[Pulsar|pulsar]] PSR B1257+12.

Hypothetical planets beyond the orbit of [[Neptune]]. Percival Lowell's search for "Planet X" appeared to be validated by Clyde Tombaugh's 1930 discovery of [[Pluto|Pluto]], but the 1978 discovery of Pluto's moon Charon allowed its mass to be estimated, disproving the hypothesis. A study of [[Voyager 2|Voyager 2]] measurements in the early 1990s found that irregularities in Uranus's orbit were due to a slight overestimation of Neptune's mass. In 2006 the International Astronomical Union reclassified Pluto as a [[Dwarf planet|dwarf planet]]. In 2014, astronomers hypothesized a distant super-Earth or ice giant, later called [[Planet Nine|Planet Nine]].

Organisms that drift in water (or air) but cannot actively propel themselves against currents or wind. Plankton include organisms from all the major biological kingdoms, from microscopic [[Bacteria|bacteria]], archaea and [[Protozoa|protozoa]] to larger organisms such as [[Jellyfish|jellyfish]]. The term describes an ecological niche and level of motility rather than taxonomy, and comes from the Greek *planktos*, meaning "drifter" or "wanderer". Traditionally, plankton were divided into phytoplankton, which make their own food by [[Photosynthesis|photosynthesis]], and zooplankton, which eat other organisms; a third group, mixoplankton, combines both modes. Phytoplankton produce roughly half of Earth's [[Oxygen|oxygen]] and play a major role in carbon sequestration. Marine microorganisms have been estimated to make up 70 to 90 percent of ocean biomass. Airborne plankton include plant spores, [[Pollen|pollen]] and wind-scattered seeds.

Study of the internal structure of plants. Originally it included [[Plant morphology|plant morphology]], the description of external form, but since the mid-20th century it has referred only to internal structure. It is now often investigated at the cellular level, using sectioning of tissues and microscopy. Classical divisions cover flower anatomy; [[Leaf|leaf]] anatomy, including the epidermis, [[Stoma|stomata]] and palisade cells; stem anatomy; fruit and seed anatomy; [[Wood|wood]] anatomy; and [[Root|root]] anatomy. The field became a modern science in the late 1600s. Italian doctor and microscopist Marcello Malpighi published *Anatomia Plantarum* in 1671. British doctor Nehemiah Grew, credited with recognizing plant cells (which he called "vesicles" and "bladders"), published *An Idea of a Philosophical History of Plants* in 1672. Theophrastus had written plant treatises about 300 BC.

Science of changing the traits of plants to produce desired characteristics. It is used to improve the quality of plant products for humans and animals, and aims to produce [[Crop|crop]] varieties with superior traits, such as tolerance to biotic and abiotic stress, grain or biomass yield, and end-use quality. Techniques range from selecting plants for propagation to methods using knowledge of genetics and chromosomes, and to more complex molecular techniques. It is practiced by gardeners and farmers, and by professional breeders at government institutions, universities and research centers. A 2023 study found that without plant breeding, Europe would have produced 20% fewer arable crops over the last 20 years, consuming an additional 21.6 million hectares of land. Plant breeding began with the [[Domestication|domestication]] of the first agricultural plants an estimated 9,000 to 11,000 years ago. [[Gregor Mendel|Gregor Mendel]]'s experiments with plant hybridization led to his laws of inheritance, and [[Selective breeding|selective breeding]] played a crucial role in the [[Green Revolution|Green Revolution]] of the 20th century.
